title: US Passport Drops to 10th in Global Rankings After Two Decades of Decline
excerpt: The Henley Passport Index's 20th-anniversary report shows the American passport, once the world's most powerful, now trails 36 countries in travel freedom.
body:
Key Takeaways
  • The US passport is now 10th globally, down from 1st in 2014.
  • Singapore leads with 192 visa-free destinations, followed by Japan, South Korea, and UAE at 188.
  • US decline attributed to Brazil, China, Vietnam, and Somalia reinstating visa requirements.
  • India's passport rose to 75th with access to 56 destinations, narrowing the gap with the US.
US Passport's Decline: A 20-Year Journey
2006
US passport ranked 1st alongside Denmark and Finland.
2014
US passport shares 1st place with the UK.
2023
US passport drops to 10th place with access to 180 destinations.
  • The US passport now ranks 10th on the Henley Passport Index with visa-free access to 180 of 227 destinations, down from the No. 1 spot it held in 2014.
  • Singapore leads the 2026 index with 192 visa-free destinations, followed by Japan, South Korea, and the UAE at 188 each.
  • The US decline was driven by Brazil reinstating visa requirements, China excluding the US from its expanding visa-free list, and similar moves by Vietnam and Somalia.
  • India's passport climbed to 75th with access to 56 destinations, up 10 spots from 2025, narrowing the gap with the United States.

The US passport has fallen to 10th place on the Henley Passport Index, its lowest ranking in the index's 20-year history, according to the 20th-anniversary report released on Monday. Once the undisputed king of global travel documents, the American passport now provides visa-free access to just 180 of 227 destinations worldwide — with 36 countries ranked ahead of it.

From No. 1 to No. 10 in Two Decades

In 2006, when the Henley Passport Index first launched, the US passport sat at the top of the rankings alongside Denmark and Finland. In 2014, it shared the No. 1 spot with the United Kingdom. The slide since then has been steady.

Singapore now holds the top position with 192 visa-free destinations, a gain of 70 since 2006. Japan, South Korea, and the United Arab Emirates share second place at 188 each. The UAE has been the index's most dramatic success story, adding 153 new visa-free destinations over two decades.

> **"Nations that embrace openness and cooperation are surging ahead, while those resting on past privilege are being left behind."

— Dr."**

A separate analysis by Global Citizen Solutions paints an even bleaker picture. On its Global Passport Index, the US dropped from first place in 2021 to 12th in 2026 — the steepest recorded decline of any G7 country. The US mobility rank on that index collapsed from 10th to 41st in just five years.

What Drove the Decline

The erosion of American passport power traces to specific policy decisions by other nations. Brazil reinstated visa requirements for American citizens in April 2025 over reciprocity concerns. China expanded its visa-free travel list to include many European and Asian nations but pointedly excluded the United States. Vietnam and Somalia also left the US off their latest visa-free expansions.

"The declining strength of the US passport over the past decade is more than just a reshuffle in rankings — it signals a fundamental shift in global mobility and soft power dynamics. Nations that embrace openness and cooperation are surging ahead, while those resting on past privilege are being left behind."

— Dr. Christian H. Kaelin, Chairman of Henley & Partners

Dr. Laura Madrid, a lead researcher at Global Citizen Solutions, noted that the practical impact is already being felt. "Destinations that were once straightforward — show up, get stamped, go — now require visas or pre-authorizations that didn't exist before," she told TravelPulse.

A Harris Poll survey of more than 6,000 Americans, conducted between August 2024 and February 2025, found that 42 percent had considered or were planning to relocate abroad, citing travel freedom among their motivations. Among younger Americans, the numbers were even higher.

"Americans are increasingly treating a second citizenship or residency not as an extravagance but as an insurance policy — a rational response to a passport whose trajectory, for the first time in living memory, is downward."

— Dr. Laura Madrid, Global Citizen Solutions

Where India Stands

For Indian-Americans, the erosion of US passport power adds a new dimension to an already complex relationship with travel documents. India's passport climbed to 75th on the Henley Index this year, up from 85th in 2025, with visa-free access to 56 destinations. While the 124-destination gap between the US and Indian passports remains significant, it has been narrowing as the US slips and India climbs.

Indian nationals who obtained US citizenship partly for the travel advantages of an American passport may find that calculus gradually shifting. India's own diplomatic efforts — expanding bilateral visa agreements and cultivating trade relationships across Asia and Africa — have produced steady gains in passport strength over the past two years.

The Henley report notes a strong correlation between peacefulness and passport power, with the most peaceful nations generally holding the strongest passports. The US is a stark outlier — ranking 10th on the passport index but 134th on the Global Peace Index.

Whether the US can arrest its decline depends on bilateral visa negotiations and its broader diplomatic approach. The gap between the world's most and least mobile citizens has widened to 118 destinations — with Afghanistan still at the bottom, as it has been for all 20 years of the index's existence. As Kaelin put it, passport strength ultimately reflects "the value other countries place on their relationship with you."
